title: On and se: speaking in general
topic: impersonal on; pronominal passive; ça se fait
why: French rarely uses the passive to talk about what people generally do: it prefers on and pronominal verbs like ça se fait or ça ne se dit pas. This lesson teaches these structures through French customs and etiquette, from la bise to table manners.

On: people in general

You have used on since the start as an everyday “we”: On va au cinéma ? But on has a second, very common meaning: people in general. English expresses this idea with “you”, “they”, “people”, “one”… or with a passive.

Ici, on parle français.French is spoken here. / We speak French here.
En France, on dîne vers vingt heures.In France, people have dinner around 8 p.m.
On dit que ce restaurant est le meilleur de Lyon.They say this restaurant is the best in Lyon.
On ne sait jamais.You never know.

Whatever its meaning, on always takes the verb in the third person singular, like il or elle: on parle, on dit, on fait, on peut.

Three meanings of on

meaningexampleEnglish
weOn part demain.We're leaving tomorrow.
people in generalEn Bretagne, on mange des crêpes.In Brittany, people eat crêpes.
someoneOn a sonné.Someone rang the doorbell.

The third meaning replaces many English passives: On m'a volé mon vélo (my bike was stolen), On m'a dit que le musée était fermé (I was told the museum was closed). French prefers an active sentence with on to a passive.

When an English sentence starts with “You…” but means anybody (“You can't park here”), think on: On ne peut pas stationner ici. Using tu or vous there would sound as if you were talking about the listener personally.

", "

Se: “it's done”, “it's said”

French has another way to express a general rule or habit: a pronominal verb with a thing as the subject. English uses a passive (“it's eaten cold”), French uses se + verb.

FrenchEnglish
Ça se mange froid.It's eaten cold.
Ce vin se boit frais.This wine is drunk chilled.
Le français se parle dans trente pays.French is spoken in thirty countries.
Comment ça se dit en français ?How do you say that in French?
Ça s'écrit comment ?How is it spelled?
Ça ne se dit pas.You don't say that.

The verb agrees with its subject: le fromage se mange, but les huîtres se mangent crues (oysters are eaten raw). And the negation goes around se + verb: ça ne se dit pas.

Ça se fait / ça ne se fait pas

This is the key expression for talking about etiquette. Ça se fait means “it's the done thing, it's normal”; ça ne se fait pas means “it's not done, it's rude”.

Apporter des fleurs quand on est invité ? Oui, ça se fait.Bringing flowers when you're invited? Yes, that's what people do.
Mettre le pain sur l'assiette ? Non, ça ne se fait pas en France.Putting the bread on your plate? No, that's not done in France.

Don't confuse this se with the reflexive verbs you know (je me lève). Here, the thing doesn't do anything to itself: ça se mange doesn't mean “it eats itself”! It means people eat it.

", "

Customs, rules and signs

To state a rule, French also uses impersonal phrases with il, which means nobody in particular: Il faut + infinitive (you have to) and Il est interdit de + infinitive (it is forbidden to). Learn il est interdit de with its de as a fixed expression. On signs, you often just read Interdit de fumer or Interdiction de stationner.

Il est interdit de fumer dans les gares.Smoking is not allowed in train stations.
Dans un magasin, il faut toujours dire bonjour.In a shop, you always have to say hello.

A few French customs

customin French
greeting friendsOn se fait la bise: two kisses in Paris, three or four in some regions.
at a dinner partyOn apporte du vin, des fleurs ou un dessert. But not chrysanthemums: they are for funerals.
arrivingOn arrive avec un petit quart d'heure de retard: arriving early is awkward.
at the tableLe pain se pose sur la table, and on garde les mains sur la table.
the cheeseLe fromage se mange après le plat et avant le dessert.

La bise is the light kiss on the cheek between friends, family, and often colleagues. With strangers and in formal situations, on se serre la main (people shake hands). If you are not sure, wait for the other person to lean in.

All these sentences use on or se because they describe what people in general do. They are perfect for comparing cultures: Chez moi, ça ne se fait pas ! or Aux États-Unis, on dîne plus tôt.
